questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Animal phyla from body plan and circulation
questions.question: An animal is triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and coelomate. Its body shows metameric segmentation, it has a closed circulatory system, and it excretes through nephridia. To which phylum does it belong?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Annelida.
Why: Each clue narrows the choice. A true coelom rules out acoelomate and pseudocoelomate animals. Metameric segmentation, in which the body is divided into similar ring-like segments, is the mark of annelids such as the earthworm and leech. A closed circulatory system, where blood stays inside vessels, and nephridia for excretion and osmoregulation complete the description of Annelida.
Why not the others: (A) Platyhelminthes are acoelomate flatworms without a circulatory system; they excrete through flame cells. (B) Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomate roundworms and are not segmented. (C) Arthropods are segmented coelomates, but their circulatory system is open and they excrete through Malpighian tubules.
Key point: Annelida: metameric segments, closed circulation, nephridia.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: From the frog-heart figure, trace the labelled inflow vessels P and Q through the chambers. Which deduction about circulation is justified?
options: A) The ventricle receives both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor streams
B) P brings oxygen-poor blood and Q oxygen-rich blood
C) Frogs have two fully separated ventricles
D) Blood from P bypasses the ventricle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The ventricle receives both streams.
Why: Gas exchange in the lungs enriches returning blood in P, whereas systemic venous blood in Q is relatively oxygen-poor. The two atria connect to one ventricle, so anatomical separation at the ventricular level is incomplete; this does not mean all outflow is uniformly mixed.
Why not the others: (B) reverses both return routes; (C) contradicts the drawn single ventricle; (D) ignores the left atrium's outlet.
Key point: Trace inflow routes and oxygenation through the chambers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A cultured diploid cell shows the chromosome and DNA pattern X in the figure. At which stage is this pattern expected before sister-chromatid separation?
options: D) Gamete maturation after meiosis II
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) G2 after replication.
Why: Replication doubles the DNA from 2C to 4C while each pair of sister chromatids remains joined at one centromere. Chromosome count by centromeres stays 2n in G2; the drawn pattern is not a doubling of chromosome number.
Why not the others: (A) is 2C; (B) separates centromeres so the chromosome count changes within the cell; (D) yields haploid products with different content.
Key point: Count chromosomes by centromeres and DNA by molecule content.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis
questions.question: In photosynthesis by green plants, from which substance does the oxygen gas that is released come?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Water.
Why: In the light reaction, water is split at photosystem II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The electrons replace those lost by the chlorophyll of photosystem II, the protons add to the gradient used to make ATP, and the oxygen is given off. Experiments with water labelled with the isotope ¹⁸O showed that the labelled oxygen appears in the O₂ released.
Why not the others: (B) The oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide end up in the sugar and in new water molecules, not in the O₂ gas. (C) Glucose is a product of photosynthesis and is not broken down in the process. (D) Chlorophyll absorbs light and passes on electrons; it does not supply oxygen atoms.
Key point: O₂ comes from the splitting of water at photosystem II.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A skeletal-muscle fibre receives Ca²⁺ but a drug prevents myosin heads from binding actin. Which immediate event is blocked while the thin filament can still expose its sites?
options: D) Cross-bridge formation and force generation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cross-bridge formation and force generation.
Why: Contraction follows a fixed order. A nerve signal depolarises the sarcolemma, Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the binding sites on actin. Only then can the myosin heads attach to actin, form cross-bridges and pull the thin filaments. The drug acts at this last step, so the sites are exposed but no cross-bridges form and no force develops.
Why not the others: (A) ATP synthesis in mitochondria does not depend on myosin binding to actin. (B) Ca²⁺ has been supplied and can still bind troponin; the stem says the sites are exposed. (C) Depolarisation of the sarcolemma happens before Ca²⁺ release and is not affected.
Key point: Ca²⁺ → troponin → sites exposed → cross-bridges → sliding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A primary spermatocyte has 2n=46 chromosomes and has completed DNA replication. After meiosis I, each secondary spermatocyte has which chromosome and chromatid counts?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids.
Why: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, so each secondary spermatocyte gets one chromosome of each pair: 23 chromosomes, a haploid set. The sister chromatids have not yet separated, so each of those 23 chromosomes still consists of two chromatids, giving 46 chromatids. They separate in meiosis II, when each spermatid receives 23 single-chromatid chromosomes.
Why not the others: (A) 46 chromosomes would mean the homologues did not separate. (C) 23 chromatids is the state after meiosis II, in a spermatid. (D) 46 chromosomes with 92 chromatids is the primary spermatocyte before meiosis I.
Key point: After meiosis I: n chromosomes, each with two chromatids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A coding-strand DNA triplet 5′-TAC-3′ is transcribed. Which mRNA codon and amino acid follow, using AUG=Met and UAC=Tyr?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5′-UAC-3′, Tyr.
Why: The coding strand of DNA has the same sequence as the mRNA, except that thymine is replaced by uracil, because the mRNA is copied from the complementary template strand. So coding-strand 5′-TAC-3′ gives the codon 5′-UAC-3′, which codes for tyrosine.
Why not the others: (B) 5′-AUG-3′ would be made if TAC were on the template strand read 3′ to 5′; the stem says it is the coding strand. (C) writes the codon with the wrong polarity. (D) keeps thymine, which does not occur in mRNA.
Key point: mRNA = coding strand with U in place of T.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: During the first few days of breastfeeding, a newborn receives antibodies (mainly IgA) in the mother's colostrum. What type of immunity does this give the infant?
options: A) Active immunity, because the infant's own B cells make the antibodies
B) Active immunity produced artificially, as by a vaccine
C) Innate immunity from physical barriers
D) Passive immunity, because ready-made antibodies are received
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Passive immunity, because ready-made antibodies are received.
Why: Immunity is passive when the body is given antibodies made by another individual instead of making its own. Colostrum, the yellowish milk of the first days, is rich in IgA antibodies that protect the infant's gut. The fetus also receives IgG antibodies across the placenta. This protection acts at once but lasts only a short time, because no memory cells are formed in the infant.
Why not the others: (A) In active immunity the person's own lymphocytes respond to an antigen and make antibodies; here the antibodies come from the mother. (B) Vaccination introduces an antigen so that the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells; no antigen is given here. (C) Innate immunity consists of non-specific barriers such as skin, mucus and phagocytes, not specific antibodies.
Key point: Active: the body makes antibodies (slow, long-lasting). Passive: antibodies are supplied (immediate, short-lived).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure compares antibiotic-selected colonies X and Y before and after induction. Which observation establishes successful expression rather than mere plasmid uptake?
options: B) X's protein band at the expected mass after induction
C) Y's lack of an unrelated colony colour
D) Equal sizes of X and Y colonies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X's induced protein band.
Why: Antibiotic survival selects cells that carry resistance but does not show transcription or translation of the inserted gene. A band of the expected mass appearing upon induction in X, absent from control Y, supports expression of the target product. Identity may still require a specific assay.
Why not the others: (A) measures selection only; (C) uses an irrelevant phenotype; (D) colony size is not protein-specific evidence.
Key point: Include a product-specific comparison to claim expression.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a population, the number of pre-reproductive individuals is much larger than the number of reproductive individuals, which in turn is larger than the number of post-reproductive individuals. What does this age pyramid indicate about the population?
options: D) It has reached its carrying capacity
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It is expanding.
Why: An age pyramid shows the share of a population in the pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive age groups. When the youngest group is the largest, the pyramid has a broad base and is triangular. Many individuals will soon enter the reproductive age, so births will exceed deaths and the population will grow.
Why not the others: (A) A declining population has an urn-shaped pyramid, with fewer pre-reproductive than reproductive individuals. (B) A stable population has a bell-shaped pyramid, with the pre-reproductive and reproductive groups about equal. (D) At carrying capacity the growth rate is close to zero, which corresponds to a stable age structure, not a broad-based one.
Key point: Triangular: expanding. Bell-shaped: stable. Urn-shaped: declining.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 and a normal pair of sex chromosomes. Which disorder is this, and what is its usual cause?
options: A) Down's syndrome; failure of chromosome 21 to separate during gamete formation
B) Turner's syndrome; loss of one X chromosome
C) Klinefelter's syndrome; an extra X chromosome in a male
D) Phenylketonuria; a recessive mutation in one gene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Down's syndrome; failure of chromosome 21 to separate during gamete formation.
Why: An extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21) gives 47 chromosomes and causes Down's syndrome. It arises when the pair of chromosome 21 fails to separate at meiosis (nondisjunction), so a gamete carries two copies; fertilisation by a normal gamete then gives three.
Why not the others: (B) Turner's syndrome has 45 chromosomes with a single X (XO). (C) Klinefelter's syndrome also has 47 chromosomes, but the extra one is an X (XXY); here the sex chromosomes are normal. (D) Phenylketonuria is a Mendelian disorder caused by a gene mutation and shows a normal karyotype.
Key point: Trisomy 21: Down's. XO: Turner's. XXY: Klinefelter's.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A patient passes about 10 litres of very dilute urine a day and is constantly thirsty. Blood glucose is normal and the urine contains no glucose. Deficiency of which hormone best explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin).
Why: ADH from the posterior pituitary makes the distal tubules and collecting ducts permeable to water, so water is reabsorbed and the urine is concentrated. Without ADH this water is lost: the person passes large volumes of dilute urine and becomes dehydrated and thirsty. This condition is diabetes insipidus.
Why not the others: (A) Lack of insulin also causes heavy urination, but with high blood glucose and glucose in the urine, which are ruled out here. (C) Lack of aldosterone causes loss of sodium, not this pattern of very dilute urine. (D) Glucagon raises blood glucose and does not control urine volume.
Key point: No ADH: diabetes insipidus (dilute urine, normal glucose). No insulin: diabetes mellitus (glucose in urine).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A person's blood contains 15 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL, and each gram of haemoglobin can combine with about 1.34 mL of O₂. If the total blood volume is 5 L, about how much O₂ can the haemoglobin carry when fully saturated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1000 mL.
Given: Haemoglobin 15 g per 100 mL of blood; 1.34 mL O₂ per gram of haemoglobin; blood volume 5 L = 5000 mL.
Formula/Principle: O₂ capacity = haemoglobin content × O₂ bound per gram.
Step 1: O₂ per 100 mL of blood = 15 × 1.34 = 20.1 mL.
Step 2: Number of 100 mL portions in 5000 mL = 50.
Step 3: Total O₂ = 20.1 × 50 = 1005 mL, about 1000 mL.
Why: Nearly all the oxygen in blood is carried bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin; very little is dissolved in the plasma. The oxygen capacity of blood therefore follows from how much haemoglobin it contains. About 20 mL of O₂ per 100 mL is the usual figure for fully oxygenated blood.
Why not the others: (A) 20 mL is the amount in 100 mL of blood, not in 5 L. (B) 200 mL is the amount in 1 L. (D) 5000 mL is the volume of the blood itself.
Key point: Fully saturated blood carries about 20 mL O₂ per 100 mL.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Length and number of turns of a DNA double helix
questions.question: In B-form DNA, successive base pairs are 0.34 nm apart along the axis and one full turn of the helix contains 10 base pairs. For a double-stranded DNA segment of 1000 base pairs, what are its length, its number of helical turns and its number of nucleotides?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 340 nm; 100 turns; 2000 nucleotides.
Given: 1000 base pairs; rise per base pair 0.34 nm; 10 base pairs per turn.
Formula/Principle: Length = number of base pairs × rise per base pair. Turns = base pairs ÷ base pairs per turn. Each base pair has two nucleotides.
Step 1: Length = 1000 × 0.34 nm = 340 nm.
Step 2: Turns = 1000 ÷ 10 = 100.
Step 3: Nucleotides = 1000 × 2 = 2000.
Why: The two strands run side by side, so the length of the molecule depends on the number of base pairs, not on the number of nucleotides. One turn of the helix is 3.4 nm long because it holds ten pairs spaced 0.34 nm apart. Counting nucleotides needs both strands.
Why not the others: (A) 34 nm is ten times too short, and 1000 nucleotides counts only one strand. (B) 1000 turns treats each base pair as a full turn. (C) 3400 nm uses 3.4 nm, the length of a whole turn, for each base pair, and again counts one strand.
Key point: Length (nm) = base pairs × 0.34; pitch = 3.4 nm = 10 base pairs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which cells of the testis secrete testosterone, and which pituitary hormone stimulates them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Leydig cells; LH.
Why: The Leydig (interstitial) cells lie in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules and make androgens, mainly testosterone. Luteinising hormone from the anterior pituitary acts on these cells and stimulates them. The testosterone in turn supports spermatogenesis.
Why not the others: (A) Sertoli cells lie inside the tubules and nourish the developing sperm; FSH acts on them, but they do not make testosterone. (C) Spermatogonia are the germ cells that divide to form sperm; they do not secrete hormones. (D) The cell is right, but the stimulating hormone is LH, not prolactin, which controls milk formation.
Key point: LH acts on Leydig cells (androgens); FSH acts on Sertoli cells.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following species contains a coordinate (dative) bond?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) NH₄⁺.
Why: In a coordinate bond both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom. In ammonia, nitrogen has a lone pair. A hydrogen ion, H⁺, has no electrons, so nitrogen donates its lone pair to form the fourth N–H bond in the ammonium ion. Once formed, all four N–H bonds are identical.
Why not the others: (A) In methane each C–H bond is an ordinary covalent bond with one electron from each atom. (B) Sodium chloride is ionic: an electron is transferred, not shared. (C) In hydrogen each atom gives one electron to the shared pair.
Key point: Donor needs a lone pair; acceptor needs an empty orbital.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: IUPAC nomenclature of a coordination compound
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) chloride.
Why: The complex ion is the cation [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]⁺, because one chloride ion outside the bracket balances it. Water is neutral and each chlorido ligand is −1, so x + 0 − 2 = +1 and chromium is +3. Ligands are named in alphabetical order, ignoring the number prefixes: aqua before chlorido. The complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name, followed by the anion.
Why not the others: (B) Chromium(II) would make the complex neutral, with no chloride outside the bracket. (C) The ligands are in the wrong order; "aqua" comes before "chlorido". (D) Only two chlorides are ligands; the third is a counter-ion and is named separately as chloride.
Key point: Ligands alphabetically, then metal with oxidation state, then the counter-ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Using the metal-and-water calorimeter data in the figure, and neglecting heat loss and cup heat, find the metal specific heat.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.76 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Given: From the figure: 100 g of metal at 85 °C is put into 200 g of water at 25 °C; final temperature 30 °C; \(c_{\text{water}}=4.2\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water; \(q=mc\,\Delta T\).
Step 1: Water: \(q=200\times4.2\times(30-25)=4200\ \mathrm J\).
Step 2: Metal: \(q=100\times c\times(85-30)=5500c\).
Step 3: \(5500c=4200\).
Worked derivation: \[c=\frac{4200}{5500}=0.764\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\approx0.76\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\]
Why: With no heat lost to the surroundings and the cup ignored, all the heat given out by the hot metal goes into the water. The metal cools by 55 K while the water warms by only 5 K, which shows that the metal has a much smaller heat capacity.
Why not the others: (A) 0.38 is half the correct value. (C) 1.52 is twice the correct value. (D) 4.20 is the specific heat of water, not of the metal.
Key point: \(m_1c_1\Delta T_1=m_2c_2\Delta T_2\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 2.8 g of N₂ and 1.0 g of H₂ are mixed and react completely according to N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. What mass of NH₃ is formed, and what mass of H₂ is left over? (H = 1, N = 14)
options: A) 5.67 g NH₃; no H₂ left
B) 3.4 g NH₃; 0.8 g H₂ left
C) 3.4 g NH₃; 0.4 g H₂ left
D) 1.7 g NH₃; 0.7 g H₂ left
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3.4 g NH₃; 0.4 g H₂ left.
Given: 2.8 g \(\ce{N2}\) (\(M=28\)); 1.0 g \(\ce{H2}\) (\(M=2\)); \(M(\ce{NH3})=17\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}\); the reagent that runs out first fixes the amount of product.
Step 1: \(n(\ce{N2})=2.8/28=0.10\ \mathrm{mol}\); \(n(\ce{H2})=1.0/2=0.50\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: 0.10 mol \(\ce{N2}\) needs \(3\times0.10=0.30\ \mathrm{mol}\ \ce{H2}\); 0.50 mol is available, so \(\ce{N2}\) is limiting.
Step 3: \(n(\ce{NH3})=2\times0.10=0.20\ \mathrm{mol}\); \(\ce{H2}\) left \(=0.50-0.30=0.20\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Worked derivation: \[m(\ce{NH3})=0.20\times17=3.4\ \mathrm g;\qquad m(\ce{H2})_{\text{left}}=0.20\times2=0.4\ \mathrm g\]
Why: The masses must be changed to moles before they are compared, and the comparison must use the 1 : 3 ratio of the equation. Hydrogen has the smaller mass but, because its molar mass is so low, it is present in excess. A check on mass: 2.8 + 1.0 = 3.8 g before, and 3.4 + 0.4 = 3.8 g after.
Why not the others: (A) 5.67 g takes hydrogen as the limiting reagent (0.50 × 2/3 mol of NH₃), but there is not enough nitrogen for that. (B) has the right mass of ammonia but removes only 0.10 mol of H₂, using a 1 : 1 ratio. (D) 1.7 g forms only 0.10 mol of NH₃, ignoring the coefficient 2.
Key point: Divide moles by coefficients; the smallest quotient marks the limiting reagent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Standard Gibbs energy of a galvanic cell
questions.question: A galvanic cell uses the reaction Fe(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). The standard electrode potentials are E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. Taking F = 96500 C mol⁻¹, what is the standard Gibbs energy change of the cell reaction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −239 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: \(E^\circ(\ce{Fe^2+/Fe})=-0.44\ \mathrm V\); \(E^\circ(\ce{Ag+/Ag})=+0.80\ \mathrm V\); \(F=96500\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\); \(\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\).
Step 1: Silver is the cathode and iron the anode: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.80-(-0.44)=1.24\ \mathrm V\).
Step 2: \(\ce{Fe -> Fe^2+ + 2e-}\), so \(n=2\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta G^\circ=-2\times96500\times1.24=-239\,320\ \mathrm J\approx-239\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: The cell reaction is spontaneous, so its Gibbs energy change is negative; the fall in Gibbs energy is the greatest electrical work the cell can do. An electrode potential is an intensive property, so E°(Ag⁺/Ag) is not doubled even though two silver ions are reduced.
Why not the others: (A) +239 has the wrong sign; a positive value would mean the reaction does not go as written. (B) −120 uses n = 1 instead of 2. (C) −394 doubles the silver potential: \(2(0.80)+0.44=2.04\ \mathrm V\).
Key point: \(\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\); never multiply E° by the coefficients.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Basic strength of amines in water
questions.question: Which of the following is the strongest base in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (CH₃)₂NH.
Why: Methyl groups push electrons towards nitrogen (+I effect), which makes the lone pair more available, so alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia. In water a second factor matters: the protonated amine is stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water, and this is greatest when more N–H bonds are present. The tertiary ammonium ion has only one N–H and is also crowded. The balance of the two effects gives the order (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃.
Why not the others: (B) Ammonia has no electron-releasing alkyl group and is the weakest of the four. (C) Methylamine has one methyl group; it is weaker than dimethylamine. (D) Trimethylamine has the greatest inductive effect, but its cation is poorly solvated, so in water it is weaker than the secondary amine.
Key point: In water, for methylamines: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH₃.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In acidic permanganate titration, MnO₄⁻ accepts 5 electrons per ion and Fe²⁺ donates 1. How many moles of Fe²⁺ react with 0.020 mol MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.100 mol.
Given: 0.020 mol \(\ce{MnO4-}\); each \(\ce{MnO4-}\) gains 5 electrons; each \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) loses 1 electron.
Formula/Principle: Electrons gained by the oxidising agent = electrons lost by the reducing agent.
Step 1: Electrons gained \(=0.020\times5=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: Each \(\ce{Fe^2+}\) supplies one electron, so \(n(\ce{Fe^2+})=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Worked derivation: \[\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O};\qquad n(\ce{Fe^2+})=5\times0.020=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\]
Why: In acid, manganese goes from +7 in permanganate to +2, a gain of five electrons, while iron goes from +2 to +3, a loss of one. Five iron(II) ions are therefore needed for each permanganate ion.
Why not the others: (A) 0.020 mol assumes a 1 : 1 ratio. (C) 0.004 mol divides by 5 instead of multiplying. (D) 0.500 mol applies the factor of 5 twice.
Key point: n(oxidant) × electrons gained = n(reductant) × electrons lost.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows two reaction-energy profiles with the same reactants and products; path X has a lower maximum than Y. Which conclusion follows at equal temperature if both profiles represent the same overall reaction?
options: A) X has a more negative reaction enthalpy than Y
B) X has a higher reverse activation energy but the same forward one
C) X has a smaller forward activation barrier; ΔH is unchanged
D) X changes the equilibrium constant through a new energy gap
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lower barrier, same ΔH.
Why: The barrier is the vertical rise from reactants to the transition-state maximum, which is smaller for X. Because the endpoints coincide, the enthalpy difference between products and reactants does not change. A catalyst-like lower pathway can speed the kinetics without changing equilibrium thermodynamics.
Why not the others: (A) endpoint ΔH is identical; (B) reverses the indicated forward comparison; (D) equilibrium at fixed T depends on the endpoints, not path height.
Key point: Distinguish path-dependent activation energy from state-function enthalpy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO). What is the main organic product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Methane.
Why: Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime removes the carboxyl carbon as sodium carbonate; this is decarboxylation. The hydrocarbon formed has one carbon atom fewer than the acid: \(\ce{CH3COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][heat] CH4 + Na2CO3}\).
Why not the others: (A) Ethane would need the two-carbon skeleton to be kept, but one carbon is lost as carbonate. (B) Ethanol would require reduction of the acid, for example with LiAlH₄. (C) Ethanal would require partial reduction, which soda lime does not do.
Key point: RCOONa + NaOH (CaO) → R–H + Na₂CO₃: one carbon fewer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Two compounds have molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. One is butan-1-ol and the other is ethoxyethane. Their relationship is best described as?
options: A) Functional-group isomers with alcohol versus ether
B) Geometric isomers around a double bond
C) Enantiomers with the same connectivity
D) Tautomers interconverted by proton shift
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Functional-group isomers.
Why: The two molecules share formula but differ in connectivity around oxygen: one contains an O–H bond and the other a C–O–C linkage. This changes the functional group and typical reactivity while conserving atom count.
Why not the others: (B) there is no alkene geometry; (C) connectivity is not identical; (D) an alcohol–ether pair is not a proton-shift tautomeric equilibrium.
Key point: Match formula first, then locate the functional group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At the same temperature, compare dilute aqueous solution X containing 0.10 m glucose plus 0.05 m fully dissociated NaCl with solution Y containing 0.075 m fully dissociated CaCl₂. In the same solvent, what is ΔTf(Y)/ΔTf(X)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9/8.
Given: X: 0.10 m glucose + 0.05 m NaCl (fully dissociated). Y: 0.075 m \(\ce{CaCl2}\) (fully dissociated). Same solvent.
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta T_f=K_f\times\) (total molality of solute particles).
Step 1: X: glucose gives 0.10; NaCl gives \(2\times0.05=0.10\); total \(=0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}\).
Step 2: Y: \(\ce{CaCl2}\) gives \(3\times0.075=0.225\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta T_f(Y)}{\Delta T_f(X)}=\frac{0.225K_f}{0.20K_f}=\frac98\]
Why: Freezing-point depression depends on the number of dissolved particles. Glucose stays as one particle, NaCl gives two ions and CaCl₂ gives three. Solution Y has the lower formula concentration but more particles, so it freezes at a slightly lower temperature.
Why not the others: (A) 3/4 = 0.075/0.10 compares only the CaCl₂ and glucose molalities. (B) 1 treats the two particle totals as equal. (C) 8/9 is the ratio upside down.
Key point: Add up i × m for every solute.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Volume of base needed to neutralise a diprotic acid
questions.question: What volume of 0.10 M NaOH is needed to neutralise 25.0 mL of 0.20 M H₂SO₄ completely?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 100 mL.
Given: 25.0 mL of 0.20 M \(\ce{H2SO4}\); 0.10 M NaOH.
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O}\); 1 mol acid needs 2 mol base.
Step 1: \(n(\ce{H2SO4})=0.0250\ \mathrm L\times0.20\ \mathrm M=0.0050\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: \(n(\ce{NaOH})=2\times0.0050=0.010\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Worked derivation: \[V(\ce{NaOH})=\frac{0.010\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}}=0.100\ \mathrm L=100\ \mathrm{mL}\]
Why: Sulfuric acid is diprotic: each molecule gives two hydrogen ions, so it needs two hydroxide ions. The base is also half as concentrated as the acid, so four times the volume is needed in all.
Why not the others: (B) 50 mL treats the acid as monoprotic. (C) 25 mL assumes equal volumes react. (D) 200 mL applies the factor of two twice.
Key point: \(n_aM_aV_a=n_bM_bV_b\), with n the number of H⁺ or OH⁻ per formula unit.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Between F and Cl, which element has the more negative first electron-gain enthalpy in the usual atomic comparison, and why?
options: A) F, because its atomic radius is smaller
B) Cl, because its larger 3p region reduces electron–electron crowding
C) They are equal because both are halogens
D) Neither accepts an electron exothermically
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cl.
Why: Fluorine's compact 2p valence region creates stronger repulsion for an arriving electron; chlorine's more spacious 3p shell can accommodate it with a larger energy release. This is an exception to a simplistic size-only trend.
Why not the others: (A) ignores compact-orbital repulsion; (C) shared group does not force identical enthalpy; (D) both electron gains can be exothermic.
Key point: Orbital crowding can outweigh a monotonic periodic trend.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A short double-stranded DNA region has 24 base pairs, of which 9 are A–T pairs. How many G–C pairs and total hydrogen bonds does this region contain if A–T has two and G–C three bonds?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 15 G–C pairs; 63 bonds.
Given: 24 base pairs in all; 9 are A–T. A–T has 2 hydrogen bonds; G–C has 3.
Formula/Principle: G–C pairs = total − A–T pairs. Hydrogen bonds = 2 × (A–T pairs) + 3 × (G–C pairs).
Step 1: G–C pairs \(=24-9=15\).
Step 2: Hydrogen bonds \(=2(9)+3(15)=18+45\).
Worked derivation: \[n_{GC}=24-9=15;\qquad N_H=2(9)+3(15)=63\]
Why: Every base pair is either A–T or G–C, so the two kinds add up to the total. Adenine and thymine are held by two hydrogen bonds, guanine and cytosine by three; this is why DNA rich in G–C is harder to separate into single strands.
Why not the others: (A) has the right number of pairs but counts only the G–C bonds (45). (B) takes 9 as the number of G–C pairs. (D) treats all 24 pairs as G–C.
Key point: H bonds = 2(A–T) + 3(G–C).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are heated in a 1.0 L vessel. At equilibrium the vessel contains 1.6 mol of HI, formed by H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What is K_c?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 64.
Given: 1.0 mol \(\ce{H2}\) and 1.0 mol \(\ce{I2}\) in 1.0 L; 1.6 mol HI at equilibrium.
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}\); \(K_c=\dfrac{[\ce{HI}]^2}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{I2}]}\).
Step 1: Forming 1.6 mol HI uses \(1.6/2=0.80\ \mathrm{mol}\) of each reactant.
Step 2: \([\ce{H2}]=[\ce{I2}]=1.0-0.80=0.20\ \mathrm M\); \([\ce{HI}]=1.6\ \mathrm M\).
Worked derivation: \[K_c=\frac{(1.6)^2}{(0.20)(0.20)}=\frac{2.56}{0.040}=64\]
Why: Two molecules of HI form from one of H₂ and one of I₂, so the reactants used are half the HI formed. The HI concentration is squared because its coefficient is 2. The numbers of gas molecules are equal on both sides, so K_c has no units and does not depend on the volume.
Why not the others: (A) 8 = 1.6/0.20 leaves out the square and one reactant. (B) 16 takes [HI] as 0.80 M, the amount of H₂ used. (D) 2.56 is only the numerator, [HI]².
Key point: Set out initial, change and equilibrium amounts before substituting.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A circle tangent to both coordinate axes lies in the first quadrant and passes through (4,2). Which pair gives all possible radii?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 and 10.
Given: \(\text{circle tangent to both axes, first quadrant, through }(4,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{centre }(r,r),\quad(x-r)^2+(y-r)^2=r^2\)
Step 1: \((4-r)^2+(2-r)^2=r^2\)
Step 2: \(16-8r+r^2+4-4r+r^2=r^2\Rightarrow r^2-12r+20=0\)
Worked derivation: \[(r-2)(r-10)=0\Rightarrow r=2\ \text{or}\ r=10\]
Check: \[r=2:\ (4-2)^2+0=4;\qquad r=10:\ (-6)^2+(-8)^2=100\]
Why: \(\text{tangent to both axes}\Rightarrow|x_c|=|y_c|=r\)
Why not the others: (B) \(r=10\ \text{also satisfies the equation}\); (C) \(r=4:\ 0+4\ne16\); (D) \(r=2\ \text{also satisfies the equation}\).
Key point: \(\text{circle touching both axes: centre }(r,r)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Origin chord constrained by line-circle intersections
questions.question: The circle \(x^2+y^2=4x\) and the line \(y=kx\) meet at the origin and at P. If OP has length 2, what are all possible real k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ±√3.
Given: \(x^2+y^2=4x,\quad y=kx,\quad OP=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{substitute the line into the circle}\)
Step 1: \(x^2(1+k^2)=4x\Rightarrow x_P=\dfrac{4}{1+k^2}\ \ (x\ne0)\)
Step 2: \(y_P=\dfrac{4k}{1+k^2}\)
Step 3: \(OP=\sqrt{x_P^2+y_P^2}=\dfrac{4\sqrt{1+k^2}}{1+k^2}=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{1+k^2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{4}{\sqrt{1+k^2}}=2\Rightarrow1+k^2=4\Rightarrow k=\pm\sqrt3\]
Check: \[\text{diameter}=4,\ OP=4\cos\theta=2\Rightarrow\theta=60^\circ,\ k=\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3\]
Why: \(O\ \text{lies on the circle};\ \text{chord through }O\ \text{at angle }\theta:\ OP=2R\cos\theta\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=\pm1:\ OP=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt2}=2\sqrt2\); (C) \(k=\pm2:\ OP=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt5}\); (D) \(k=0:\ OP=4\).
Key point: \(OP=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{1+k^2}}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordinate geometry: circle and straight line

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of horizontal-line intersections on monotone branches
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) restricted to \([-2,2]\), for which real k does the horizontal line \(y=k\) meet the graph at exactly three distinct points?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \((-2,2)\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-3x,\quad x\in[-2,2]\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)=3(x-1)(x+1)\)
Step 1: \(f(-2)=-2,\quad f(-1)=2,\quad f(1)=-2,\quad f(2)=2\)
Step 2: \([-2,-1]:\ f\uparrow\ -2\to2;\quad[-1,1]:\ f\downarrow\ 2\to-2;\quad[1,2]:\ f\uparrow\ -2\to2\)
Step 3: \(-2<k<2:\ \text{one root in each of }(-2,-1),\ (-1,1),\ (1,2)\)
Step 4: \(k=2:\ x=-1,\ 2\ (\text{two});\quad k=-2:\ x=-2,\ 1\ (\text{two})\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{three distinct points}\iff-2<k<2\]
Check: \[k=0:\ x^3-3x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pm\sqrt3\in[-2,2]\]
Why: \(\text{each monotone branch covers }[-2,2]\ \text{once}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=\pm2:\ \text{two points}\); (B) \(k=-3:\ \text{no point in }[-2,2]\); (D) \(k=3:\ \text{no point in }[-2,2]\).
Key point: \(\text{count one root per monotone branch}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differentiation: increasing decreasing functions and extrema

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate \(\int_1^2 \dfrac{x^2+1}{x(x+1)^2}\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ln2−1/3.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_1^2\frac{x^2+1}{x(x+1)^2}\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{x^2+1}{x(x+1)^2}=\dfrac Ax+\dfrac{B}{x+1}+\dfrac{C}{(x+1)^2}\)
Step 1: \(x^2+1=A(x+1)^2+Bx(x+1)+Cx\)
Step 2: \(x=0:\ A=1;\quad x=-1:\ 2=-C\Rightarrow C=-2;\quad x^2:\ 1=A+B\Rightarrow B=0\)
Step 3: \(I=\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(\frac1x-\frac{2}{(x+1)^2}\right)dx=\left[\ln x+\frac{2}{x+1}\right]_1^2\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\left(\ln2+\frac23\right)-\left(0+1\right)=\ln2-\frac13\approx0.360\]
Check: \[\frac1x-\frac{2}{(x+1)^2}=\frac{(x+1)^2-2x}{x(x+1)^2}=\frac{x^2+1}{x(x+1)^2}\]
Why: \(\text{repeated linear factor}\Rightarrow\text{terms in }\dfrac{1}{x+1}\ \text{and}\ \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\ln2+\tfrac13\) (sign of \(\tfrac23-1\)); (B) \(\ln2-\tfrac23\) (\(\left[\tfrac{2}{x+1}\right]\) lower limit omitted and sign reversed); (C) \(\ln\tfrac32=\displaystyle\int_1^2\frac{dx}{x+1}\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2}=-\frac{1}{x+1}+C\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Inverse value of a rational map
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=(2x+1)/(x-1)\), with real domain \(x\ne1\). What is \(f^{-1}(3)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4.
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-1},\quad x\ne1\)
Formula/Principle: \(f^{-1}(3)=x\iff f(x)=3\)
Step 1: \(2x+1=3(x-1)=3x-3\)
Worked derivation: \[x=4\]
Check: \[f(4)=\frac{9}{3}=3\]
Why: \(f\ \text{is one-one on }x\ne1\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=1\notin\text{domain}\); (C) \(f(2)=5\ne3\); (D) \(f(3)=\tfrac72\ne3\).
Key point: \(f^{-1}(y)=\dfrac{y+1}{y-2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real t is \(\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\4&t\end{pmatrix}\) not invertible?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) t=−2 or 2.
Given: \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\4&t\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(M\ \text{not invertible}\iff\det M=0\)
Step 1: \(\det M=t^2-4\)
Worked derivation: \[t^2-4=0\Rightarrow t=\pm2\]
Check: \[t=2:\ (4,2)=2\,(2,1);\qquad t=-2:\ (4,-2)=-2\,(-2,1)\]
Why: \(\det M=0\iff\text{rows proportional}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(t=-2:\ \det M=0\ \text{also}\); (C) \(t=\pm4:\ \det M=12\ne0\); (D) \(t=\pm2\in\mathbb R\).
Key point: \(\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: An urn has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two are drawn in order without replacement. Given that the second ball is red, what is the probability that the first was also red?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/2.
Given: \(3R,\ 2B;\ \text{two drawn in order without replacement}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(R_1|R_2)=\dfrac{P(R_1\cap R_2)}{P(R_2)}\)
Step 1: \(P(R_1\cap R_2)=\dfrac35\cdot\dfrac24=\dfrac{3}{10}\)
Step 2: \(P(R_2)=\dfrac35\cdot\dfrac24+\dfrac25\cdot\dfrac34=\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}=\dfrac35\)
Worked derivation: \[P(R_1|R_2)=\frac{3/10}{3/5}=\frac12\]
Check: \[\text{given }R_2,\ \text{the other 4 balls are }2R,2B\Rightarrow P(R_1)=\frac24\]
Why: \(P(R_2)=P(R_1)=\tfrac35\ \ (\text{symmetry of positions})\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac35=P(R_1)\) (condition ignored); (B) \(\tfrac25=P(B_1)\); (D) \(\tfrac24\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14\).
Key point: \(P(R_1|R_2)=P(R_2|R_1)\ \text{when}\ P(R_1)=P(R_2)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The coefficients of x² and x³ in (1+x)ⁿ have ratio 3:4. What is the coefficient of x⁴ in (1+2x)ⁿ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 240.
Given: \(\dbinom n2:\dbinom n3=3:4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{\binom n2}{\binom n3}=\dfrac{3}{n-2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{3}{n-2}=\dfrac34\Rightarrow n=6\)
Step 2: \([x^4]\,(1+2x)^6=\dbinom64\,2^4\)
Worked derivation: \[15\times16=240\]
Check: \[\binom62=15,\ \binom63=20,\ 15:20=3:4\]
Why: \(T_{r+1}=\dbinom nr(2x)^r\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dbinom64\cdot2^2=60\); (B) \(\dbinom64\cdot2^3=120\); (C) \(\dbinom64\cdot2^5=480\).
Key point: \([x^r](1+ax)^n=\dbinom nra^r\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Recover a square sequence from increments
questions.question: A sequence has \(a_1=1\) and \(a_{n+1}-a_n=2n+1\) for every positive integer n. What is the sum of its first ten terms?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 385.
Given: \(a_1=1,\quad a_{n+1}-a_n=2n+1\)
Formula/Principle: \(a_n=a_1+\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_{j+1}-a_j)\)
Step 1: \(a_n=1+\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(2j+1)=1+(n-1)n+(n-1)=n^2\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{10}n^2=\frac{10\cdot11\cdot21}{6}\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum_{n=1}^{10}a_n=385\]
Check: \[a_n=1,4,9,16,\dots;\quad a_{n+1}-a_n=(n+1)^2-n^2=2n+1\]
Why: \(\text{sum of the first }n\ \text{odd numbers}=n^2\)
Why not the others: (B) \(100=a_{10}\); (C) \(55=\displaystyle\sum n\); (D) \(505\ne385\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and series: special finite square sums

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}(e^{3x}-1)/x\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3.
Given: \(L=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{3x}-1}{x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\frac{e^u-1}{u}=1\)
Step 1: \(u=3x:\ \dfrac{e^{3x}-1}{x}=3\cdot\dfrac{e^u-1}{u}\)
Worked derivation: \[L=3\times1=3\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}e^{3x}\Big|_{x=0}=3\]
Why: \(e^{3x}=1+3x+\dots\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\) (factor 3 omitted); (C) \(e^0-1=0\) (denominator ignored); (D) \(\tfrac00\ \text{is not}\ \infty\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{ax}-1}{x}=a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A line has direction vector (1,2,2), and a plane has normal (2,−1,2). What is the sine of their acute angle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4/9.
Given: \(\mathbf d=(1,2,2),\quad\mathbf n=(2,-1,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2-2+4=4\)
Step 2: \(|\mathbf d|=3,\quad|\mathbf n|=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin\theta=\frac{4}{3\times3}=\frac49\]
Check: \[\cos\angle(\mathbf d,\mathbf n)=\frac49\Rightarrow\theta=90^\circ-\cos^{-1}\frac49\]
Why: \(\text{angle with the plane}=90^\circ-\text{angle with the normal}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac23=\dfrac{6}{9}\ne\dfrac49\); (B) \(\dfrac{2}{9}\) (\(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2\), last term omitted); (D) \(\dfrac{8}{9}\) (\(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2+2+4\), sign error).
Key point: \(\text{line–plane angle uses }\sin\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA have no two A's adjacent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 12.
Given: \(\text{BANANA}:\ A^3,\ N^2,\ B^1;\ \text{no two A's adjacent}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{arrange the other letters, then put the A's in the gaps}\)
Step 1: \(\text{B, N, N}:\ \dfrac{3!}{2!}=3\ \text{arrangements}\)
Step 2: \(\text{gaps}:\ 4;\quad\text{choose 3 for the A's}:\ \dbinom43=4\)
Worked derivation: \[3\times4=12\]
Check: \[\text{total}=\frac{6!}{3!\,2!}=60\ \ge12\]
Why: \(\text{at most one A per gap}\Rightarrow\text{no two A's adjacent}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3!=6\) (B, N, N arranged only); (B) \(\dbinom63=20\) (positions of A only); (C) \(3!\times4=24\) (N's taken as different).
Key point: \(\text{gap method for 'no two together'}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For z=−1−√3i, what is its principal argument in (−π,π]?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −2π/3.
Given: \(z=-1-\sqrt3\,i\)
Formula/Principle: \(\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi]\)
Step 1: \(|z|=2,\quad\cos\theta=-\tfrac12,\quad\sin\theta=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\text{third quadrant}:\ \theta=\pi+\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\ \text{or}\ \tfrac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\arg z=\frac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\]
Check: \[2\left(\cos\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)+i\sin\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right)=-1-\sqrt3\,i\]
Why: \(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\notin(-\pi,\pi]\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\) (second quadrant); (C) \(-\tfrac\pi3\) (fourth quadrant); (D) \(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}>\pi\).
Key point: \(\text{third quadrant}:\ \arg z=\theta_{\text{ref}}-\pi\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Eliminate the arbitrary constant C from the family y=Cx²+1, for x≠0. Which first-order differential equation results?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) xy′=2(y−1).
Given: \(y=Cx^2+1,\quad x\ne0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{differentiate once and eliminate }C\)
Step 1: \(y'=2Cx\)
Step 2: \(C=\dfrac{y-1}{x^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y'=\frac{2(y-1)}{x}\Rightarrow xy'=2(y-1)\]
Check: \[x(2Cx)=2Cx^2=2(y-1)\]
Why: \(\text{one arbitrary constant}\Rightarrow\text{first order}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(xy'=2Cx^2\ne Cx^2\); (C) \(y'=2Cx\ne2Cx^2\); (D) \(2y=2Cx^2+2\ne2Cx^2\).
Key point: \(\text{order}=\text{number of arbitrary constants}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many x in [0,4π] satisfy 2sin²x−3sin x+1=0 and cos x≥0?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Four solutions.
Given: \(2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1=0,\quad\cos x\ge0,\quad0\le x\le4\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(2s^2-3s+1=(2s-1)(s-1)\)
Step 1: \(\sin x=1:\ x=\dfrac\pi2,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{2}\ \ (\cos x=0\ge0)\)
Step 2: \(\sin x=\dfrac12:\ x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\cos x\ge0:\ x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6}\)
Worked derivation: \[2+2=4\]
Check: \[\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}<0;\qquad\cos\frac{13\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>0\]
Why: \(\cos x=0\ \text{satisfies}\ \cos x\ge0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (\(\sin x=1\) roots omitted); (B) \(3\ne4\); (D) \(6\) (\(\cos x\ge0\) not applied).
Key point: \(\text{solve, then test each root against the side condition}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.question: Two projectiles launch simultaneously from the same level: A is thrown vertically up at 20 m s⁻¹; B, from a point 30 m horizontally away, has horizontal speed 10 m s⁻¹ and vertical speed 20 m s⁻¹ toward A. Neglect air resistance. When do their horizontal positions first coincide, and are their heights then equal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) At 3 s, equal heights.
Given: \(A:\ x=0,\ u_y=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\quad B:\ x_0=30\ \mathrm m,\ u_x=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{towards A}),\ u_y=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=x_0+u_xt,\quad y=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^2\)
Step 1: \(x_B=30-10t=0\Rightarrow t=3\ \mathrm s\)
Step 2: \(y_A=20t-\tfrac12gt^2,\quad y_B=20t-\tfrac12gt^2\Rightarrow y_A=y_B\ \forall t\)
Worked derivation: \[t=3\ \mathrm s,\qquad y_A(3)=y_B(3)=60-45=15\ \mathrm m\ \ (g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}})\]
Check: \[\text{time of flight}=\frac{2\times20}{10}=4\ \mathrm s>3\ \mathrm s\]
Why: \(\text{equal }u_y\ \text{and equal }g\Rightarrow\text{equal heights at all times}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(t=2:\ x_B=10\ \mathrm m\ne0\); (C) \(y_A=y_B\); (D) \(t=4:\ x_B=-10\ \mathrm m\).
Key point: \(\text{relative motion of two projectiles is uniform}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A constant horizontal force 12 N moves a cart at instantaneous velocity 3 m s⁻¹ along the force. What is instantaneous mechanical power delivered?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 36 W.
Given: \(F=12\ \mathrm N,\quad v=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad\mathbf F\parallel\mathbf v\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=Fv\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\theta=0\Rightarrow\cos\theta=1\)
Worked derivation: \[P=12\times3=36\ \mathrm W\]
Check: \[\mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm W\]
Why: \(P=\dfrac{dW}{dt}=F\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac Fv=4\); (B) \(F+v=15\); (D) \(12\times4=48\).
Key point: \(P=Fv\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy when the moment of inertia changes
questions.question: A body spins about a fixed axis with no external torque. Its moment of inertia changes from I to I/4, and its initial angular speed is ω. What are its final angular speed and the factor by which its rotational kinetic energy changes?
options: A) ω/4; kinetic energy becomes one quarter
D) 4ω; kinetic energy becomes four times
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4ω; kinetic energy becomes four times.
Given: \(I\to\dfrac I4,\quad\omega_i=\omega,\quad\tau_{\text{ext}}=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_i\omega_i=I_f\omega_f,\quad K=\tfrac12I\omega^2=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\)
Step 1: \(\omega_f=\dfrac{I}{I/4}\,\omega=4\omega\)
Step 2: \(K_i=\tfrac12I\omega^2\)
Step 3: \(K_f=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac I4\cdot(4\omega)^2=2I\omega^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{K_f}{K_i}=\frac{2I\omega^2}{\tfrac12I\omega^2}=4\]
Check: \[K=\frac{L^2}{2I}:\ I\to\frac I4\Rightarrow K\to4K\]
Why: \(L\ \text{conserved};\ \text{internal work increases }K\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\omega_f=\dfrac\omega4\) (ratio inverted); (B) \(\omega_f=2\omega\) (\(\sqrt4\)); (C) \(K_f=4K_i\ne K_i\).
Key point: \(L=\text{const}\Rightarrow\omega\propto\dfrac1I,\ K\propto\dfrac1I\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Ideal incompressible water flows from a wide lower pipe at speed 2 m s⁻¹ to a narrow section 1 m higher at speed 4 m s⁻¹. With ρ=1000 kg m⁻³ and g=10 m s⁻², what is p_lower−p_upper?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 16 kPa.
Given: \(v_1=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad v_2=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad h_2-h_1=1\ \mathrm m,\quad\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(p_1+\tfrac12\rho v_1^2+\rho gh_1=p_2+\tfrac12\rho v_2^2+\rho gh_2\)
Step 1: \(p_1-p_2=\tfrac12\rho\left(v_2^2-v_1^2\right)+\rho g(h_2-h_1)\)
Step 2: \(\tfrac12(1000)(16-4)=6000\ \mathrm{Pa}\)
Step 3: \(1000\times10\times1=10\,000\ \mathrm{Pa}\)
Worked derivation: \[p_1-p_2=6000+10\,000=16\,000\ \mathrm{Pa}=16\ \mathrm{kPa}\]
Check: \[\text{both terms}>0\Rightarrow p_{\text{lower}}>p_{\text{upper}}\]
Why: \(\text{steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(6\ \mathrm{kPa}\) (height term omitted); (C) \(10\ \mathrm{kPa}\) (speed term omitted); (D) \(\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2)+\rho g\,\Delta h=12+10=22\ \mathrm{kPa}\) (\(\tfrac12\) omitted).
Key point: \(\Delta p=\tfrac12\rho\,\Delta(v^2)+\rho g\,\Delta h\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two different ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure are allowed to mix in an insulated rigid vessel. No chemical reaction occurs. Which statement about entropy of the combined system is correct?
options: A) It decreases because diffusion orders molecules
B) It increases due to additional accessible mixing arrangements
C) It remains fixed because temperature is unchanged
D) It changes sign depending only on molar mass
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It increases due to additional accessible mixing arrangements.
Given: \(\text{two different ideal gases, same }T,\ p;\quad\text{insulated rigid vessel}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta S=n_1R\ln\dfrac{V}{V_1}+n_2R\ln\dfrac{V}{V_2}\)
Step 1: \(V>V_1,\ V>V_2\Rightarrow\ln\dfrac{V}{V_1}>0,\ \ln\dfrac{V}{V_2}>0\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta S=n_1R\ln\frac{V}{V_1}+n_2R\ln\frac{V}{V_2}>0\]
Check: \[n_1=n_2=1\ \mathrm{mol},\ V_1=V_2:\ \Delta S=2R\ln2\approx11.5\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\]
Why: \(\Delta U=0,\ \Delta T=0,\ \text{each gas expands into the whole volume}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\Delta S>0\); (C) \(\Delta T=0\not\Rightarrow\Delta S=0\); (D) \(\Delta S\ \text{has no molar-mass term}\).
Key point: \(\text{irreversible mixing}\Rightarrow\Delta S>0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A string fixed at both ends has its third harmonic at 120 Hz. Keeping tension and length fixed, what is the frequency of its fifth harmonic?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 200 Hz.
Given: \(f_3=120\ \mathrm{Hz},\quad\text{string fixed at both ends}\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_n=nf_1=\dfrac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu}\)
Step 1: \(f_1=\dfrac{120}{3}=40\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Worked derivation: \[f_5=5\times40=200\ \mathrm{Hz}\]
Check: \[\frac{f_5}{f_3}=\frac53\Rightarrow120\times\frac53=200\ \mathrm{Hz}\]
Why: \(L=\dfrac{n\lambda_n}{2}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(120\times\dfrac35=72\) (inverted); (B) \(120+40=160=f_4\); (D) \(120\times5=600\).
Key point: \(f_n=nf_1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy and escape check after an orbital impulse
questions.question: A satellite initially moves in a circular orbit of radius r around mass M. At one point a brief tangential impulse increases its speed to \(\sqrt{3GM/(2r)}\), without changing its position during the impulse. Ignore all other bodies. What are the increase in total mechanical energy and the bound/unbound character immediately afterwards?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(GMm/(4r)\); bound.
Given: \(\text{circular orbit of radius }r;\quad v_f=\sqrt{\dfrac{3GM}{2r}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=\tfrac12mv^2-\dfrac{GMm}{r};\quad\text{bound}\iff E<0\)
Step 1: \(v_i^2=\dfrac{GM}{r}\Rightarrow E_i=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
Step 2: \(E_f=\tfrac12m\cdot\dfrac{3GM}{2r}-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=\dfrac{3GMm}{4r}-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=-\dfrac{GMm}{4r}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta E=-\frac{GMm}{4r}-\left(-\frac{GMm}{2r}\right)=+\frac{GMm}{4r};\qquad E_f<0\Rightarrow\text{bound}\]
Check: \[v_f^2=\frac{3GM}{2r}<v_{\text{esc}}^2=\frac{2GM}{r}\]
Why: \(\text{position unchanged}\Rightarrow\Delta U=0,\ \Delta E=\Delta K\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-\dfrac{GMm}{4r}=E_f\); (B) \(E_f<0\Rightarrow\text{bound}\); (C) \(-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}=E_i\).
Key point: \(\text{bound}\iff v<\sqrt{2GM/r}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: In the charge diagram, at which listed point on the x-axis is the net electric field zero?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) x=−3a.
Given: \(+q\ \text{at }x=0,\quad-4q\ \text{at }x=3a\ \ (\text{from the figure})\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_{\text{net}}=0\iff\dfrac{kq}{r_1^2}=\dfrac{4kq}{r_2^2}\ \text{with opposite directions}\)
Step 1: \(\text{unlike charges}\Rightarrow\text{null point outside the pair, nearer the smaller charge}:\ x<0\)
Step 2: \(x=-s:\ r_1=s,\ r_2=s+3a\Rightarrow(s+3a)^2=4s^2\Rightarrow s+3a=2s\)
Worked derivation: \[s=3a\Rightarrow x=-3a\]
Check: \[\frac{kq}{(3a)^2}=\frac{4kq}{(6a)^2}=\frac{kq}{9a^2}\]
Why: \(\text{between the charges both fields point the same way}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=a:\ \text{fields add (both along }+x)\); (C) \(x=\tfrac32a:\ \text{fields add}\); (D) \(x=6a:\ \dfrac{kq}{36a^2}\ne\dfrac{4kq}{9a^2}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}=\sqrt{\dfrac{|q_2|}{|q_1|}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A capacitor C charged to voltage V is disconnected from its source and then connected in parallel, positive to positive, to an identical uncharged capacitor. What fraction of initial stored electrostatic energy remains in the two capacitors?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: \(C_1=C\ \text{at }V;\quad C_2=C\ \text{uncharged};\quad\text{isolated, joined in parallel}\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q\ \text{conserved};\quad V_f=\dfrac{Q}{C_1+C_2};\quad U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(Q=CV\Rightarrow V_f=\dfrac{CV}{2C}=\dfrac V2\)
Step 2: \(U_i=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 3: \(U_f=\tfrac12(2C)\left(\dfrac V2\right)^2=\tfrac14CV^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{U_f}{U_i}=\frac{\tfrac14CV^2}{\tfrac12CV^2}=\frac12\]
Check: \[U_i-U_f=\tfrac14CV^2\ \ (\text{dissipated as heat and radiation})\]
Why: \(\text{charge flows until the potentials are equal}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac14\) (energy of one capacitor); (C) \(1\) (no loss assumed); (D) \(2\) (energy cannot increase).
Key point: \(\text{loss}=\dfrac{C_1C_2}{2(C_1+C_2)}(V_1-V_2)^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In a conductor, free-electron density is 1.0×10²⁸ m⁻³ and drift-speed magnitude is 1.0×10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. Taking e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, what is conventional current-density magnitude?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.6×10⁵ A m⁻².
Given: \(n=1.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\quad v_d=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(J=nev_d\)
Step 1: \(J=(1.0\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(1.0\times10^{-4})\)
Worked derivation: \[J=1.6\times10^{28-19-4}=1.6\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\]
Check: \[\mathrm{m^{-3}\cdot C\cdot m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\]
Why: \(I=neAv_d\Rightarrow J=\dfrac IA\)
Why not the others: (A) \(10^{28-19-6}=10^{3}\); (B) \(10^{28-19-5}=10^{4}\); (D) \(10^{28-19-3}=10^{6}\).
Key point: \(J=nev_d\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.question: A circular current loop's radius doubles while its current halves. What happens to magnetic-field magnitude at the centre?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) One quarter.
Given: \(R\to2R,\quad I\to\dfrac I2\)
Formula/Principle: \(B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)
Step 1: \(B'=\dfrac{\mu_0(I/2)}{2(2R)}\)
Worked derivation: \[B'=\frac14\cdot\frac{\mu_0I}{2R}=\frac B4\]
Check: \[B\propto\frac IR:\ \frac{1/2}{2}=\frac14\]
Why: \(\text{each element contributes}\ dB\propto\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2},\ \text{total length}\propto R\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2B\) (\(B\propto R/I\)); (B) \(B\) (\(B\propto IR\)); (C) \(\dfrac B2\) (only one change counted).
Key point: \(B_{\text{centre}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Infer and change reactance before comparing real power
questions.question: A series AC circuit has resistance 30 Ω and initially net inductive reactance. At a fixed frequency, a 100 V rms source drives 2 A rms. An ideal capacitor is then added in series, reducing the net reactance by 30 Ω, with R and source voltage unchanged. What are the initial and final mean real powers?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 120 W; 300 W.
Given: \(R=30\ \Omega,\quad V=100\ \mathrm V,\quad I_i=2\ \mathrm A,\quad X_f=X_i-30\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(Z=\dfrac VI=\sqrt{R^2+X^2},\quad P=I^2R\)
Step 1: \(Z_i=\dfrac{100}{2}=50\ \Omega\Rightarrow X_i=\sqrt{50^2-30^2}=40\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(P_i=2^2\times30=120\ \mathrm W\)
Step 3: \(X_f=40-30=10\ \Omega\Rightarrow Z_f^2=30^2+10^2=1000\ \Omega^2\)
Step 4: \(I_f^2=\dfrac{100^2}{1000}=10\ \mathrm{A^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[P_f=I_f^2R=10\times30=300\ \mathrm W\]
Check: \[\cos\phi_i=\frac{30}{50}=0.6:\ 100\times2\times0.6=120\ \mathrm W;\qquad P_{\max}=\frac{V^2}{R}=333\ \mathrm W>300\ \mathrm W\]
Why: \(\text{only }R\ \text{dissipates power}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(VI=200\ \mathrm{VA}\) (apparent power for \(P_i\)); (C) \(P_f\ne200\ \mathrm W\); (D) \(\text{order reversed}\).
Key point: \(P=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2R}{R^2+X^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The ray figure places an object 5 cm in front of a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. Under the Cartesian sign convention, which image distance and nature follow?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 10 cm behind, virtual.
Given: \(u=-5\ \mathrm{cm},\quad f=-10\ \mathrm{cm}\ \ (\text{concave})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v+\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1u=-\dfrac1{10}+\dfrac15=\dfrac1{10}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=+10\ \mathrm{cm}\ \ (\text{behind the mirror, virtual})\]
Check: \[m=-\frac vu=-\frac{10}{-5}=+2\ \ (\text{upright, magnified})\]
Why: \(|u|<|f|\Rightarrow\text{virtual image}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(v=-10\ \mathrm{cm}\) (sign); (C) \(v=+5\ \mathrm{cm}\) (plane-mirror result); (D) \(v=-20\ \mathrm{cm}\).
Key point: \(\text{object between pole and focus of a concave mirror}\Rightarrow\text{virtual, enlarged}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two plane electromagnetic waves propagate in the same medium at equal frequency. If wave B has twice the electric-field amplitude of wave A, what is their mean energy-flux ratio IB/IA?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Four.
Given: \(E_{0B}=2E_{0A},\quad\text{same medium, same frequency}\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=\tfrac12\varepsilon cE_0^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{I_B}{I_A}=\left(\dfrac{E_{0B}}{E_{0A}}\right)^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{I_B}{I_A}=2^2=4\]
Check: \[B_0=\frac{E_0}{c}\Rightarrow B_{0B}=2B_{0A},\quad I\propto E_0B_0\propto4\]
Why: \(I\propto E_0^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12\) (\(I\propto E_0^{-1}\)); (B) \(2\) (\(I\propto E_0\)); (D) \(8\) (\(I\propto E_0^3\)).
Key point: \(\text{intensity}\propto(\text{amplitude})^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks around intermediate mass numbers and is lower for very light nuclei. Which process involving only light nuclei can release energy according to this curve?
options: A) Splitting light nuclei into lighter pieces
C) Fusing beyond the heavy end regardless of product
D) Fusing light nuclei toward the peak
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Fusing light nuclei toward the peak.
Given: \(\text{binding energy per nucleon }(E_b/A)\ \text{peaks near }A\approx56\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q=\displaystyle\sum_{\text{products}}E_b-\sum_{\text{reactants}}E_b\)
Step 1: \(\text{light nuclei}:\ \dfrac{E_b}{A}\ \text{rises with }A\)
Step 2: \(\text{fusion of light nuclei}\Rightarrow\text{product has larger }\dfrac{E_b}{A}\)
Worked derivation: \[Q=A\left[\left(\frac{E_b}{A}\right)_{\text{product}}-\left(\frac{E_b}{A}\right)_{\text{reactants}}\right]>0\]
Check: \[{}^2\mathrm H+{}^2\mathrm H\to{}^4\mathrm{He}:\ 4(7.1)-4(1.1)=24\ \mathrm{MeV}>0\]
Why: \(\text{energy is released when }\dfrac{E_b}{A}\ \text{increases}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{splitting light nuclei}\Rightarrow\dfrac{E_b}{A}\ \text{falls}\Rightarrow Q<0\); (B) \(Q=0\); (C) \(\text{beyond the peak}\ \dfrac{E_b}{A}\ \text{falls}\Rightarrow Q<0\).
Key point: \(\text{fusion for light nuclei, fission for heavy nuclei}\)
